meta.claim_boundary: Synthetic persona-conditioned appraisals of simulated experience; not Zurich ED staff preferences or psychological measurements.
meta.quote_selection: One prespecified synthetic interview bundle per scenario-condition-orientation cell was independently audited by Codex. Only answers passing grounding and claim-layer checks were eligible; displayed text is a verbatim excerpt.
meta.note: Scores are direct means of verified synthetic appraisal dimensions. Quotes are exact excerpts retained by an independent Codex audit, not human-reviewed material or Zurich ED staff testimony.

personas.name: Team Connector
personas.tagline: Actively maintains shared awareness and treats concise coordination as productive work.

personas.name: Focus Protector
personas.tagline: Protects task continuity and accepts interruptions when their operational value is clear.

personas.name: Patient Advocate
personas.tagline: Prioritizes patient accessibility, explanation, dignity, and continuity across handoffs.

personas.name: Vigilant Monitor
personas.tagline: Scans for weak signals, escalation risk, and gaps in situational awareness.

personas.name: Adaptive Generalist
personas.tagline: Balances competing demands and changes strategy with context rather than following one dominant priority.

quotes: The shift felt like a series of calculated trade-offs between visibility and task completion. I moved heavily between the nursing work area and the left patient rooms, treating the corridor as a transit zone rather than a social hub.

The NURSTA nurse station was the most supportive feature. It provided a central hub for substantial contact activity and mutual visibility, allowing me to efficiently coordinate with colleagues and update patient status.

Introducing semi-transparent partitions at the COCPIT station would best support my priorities by improving visibility without sacrificing acoustic privacy. This would allow for quicker assessment of colleague availability, reducing the time spent searching and enabling more efficient coordination.

The shift felt like a series of rapid context switches between patient care and coordination. I spent most of my time in the right patient-room area, but had to frequently move to the COCPIT station or circulation areas to manage workflow.
The COCPIT partitions were most supportive. They provided a transparent space for intervisibility, allowing me to see colleagues and coordinate without being fully embedded in the patient-room noise.

Adding a dedicated, semi-private huddle space near the right patient-room area would support better coordination without requiring full relocation to the COCPIT station. This would reduce the diversion cost of moving to the coordination station while maintaining focus.

The shift felt like a constant negotiation between being present with patients and being available to the team. I spent most of my time in the left patient rooms and the nursing work area, shuttling back and forth.

The patient rooms themselves were the most supportive feature. They provided fixed clinical destinations where I could complete tasks like initial assessments and discharge planning without constant interruption.

I would introduce a dedicated, semi-private huddle space near the nursing work area for quick coordination. This would allow for focused discussions without leaving the patient rooms or getting lost in the circulation area.
